Desktop terrain study · Amakhala Game Reserve · 27 September 2026
Prepared for Richard, Amakhala Game Reserve

One network across the whole reserve.

We modelled Amakhala's terrain from satellite elevation data and ran every link through a line-of-sight and Fresnel-zone check. The result: two ridge high-sites and one short relay put 8 of the 8 lodges we could locate on clear radio paths, fed from a carrier uplink on Paterson high ground.

8 of 8lodges on a clear, Fresnel-zone-clear radio path
2 + 1ridge high-sites plus short relays for lodges in valleys
66%of the 129 km² study area in line of sight for field teams and sensors
17.1 kmclear uplink path from Paterson high ground into the reserve
How it is built

Carrier in, private network out

Most lodges on Amakhala list Wi-Fi in the public areas by the main lodge, with each lodge sorting out its own connection. We propose a single backbone that belongs to the reserve.

Layer 1 · Carrier

Uplink from Paterson high ground

An uncontended business-grade Vodacom service, delivered by CTTX over a 17.1 km link from Paterson high ground to High Site North. LTE failover keeps the reserve connected if the carrier path drops.

Layer 2 · Backbone

Two ridge high-sites

High Site North (353 m) and High Site South (410 m) sit 4.5 km apart with a clear link between them. A short Safari relay serves a lodge the ridges cannot see. Each runs on solar and lithium storage with remote monitoring, so the network stays up through load-shedding.

Layer 3 · Distribution

Every lodge and ops site

Sector radios on each high site reach the lodges, HQ, the anti-poaching base, ecology, the workshop and the gates. A LoRaWAN gateway on the backbone is ready for fence, water-point, pump and fuel sensors.

Link planning

Every path checked against the terrain

Each profile below shows the ground between two sites (green), the radio path (amber line) and its first Fresnel zone (amber band). We allow for earth curvature and require at least 60% of the Fresnel zone to be clear at every point. A path that fails is not drawn on the map.

One backbone for every driver of the business

Carrier connectivity comes in once. Everything on the property runs over infrastructure the reserve owns. New cameras, sensors and lodges plug in without a new provider contract.

Guest experience

Reliable Wi-Fi, booking and card payments at every lodge.

Staff communication

Lodges, HQ, rangers and maintenance on one network, day and night.

Sandymount Safaris · 30,000+ ha, three lodges

Before

A consumer wireless service at about 3 Mbps down and 8 Mbps up, with the provider on site daily to swap IPs and reinstall equipment.

After

A Vodacom-backed 100 Mbps symmetrical link into the reserve, a CTTX-built main mast and two secondary masts, solar and lithium power, all monitored remotely.

Guest experience

HD sport streams live at the lodges. Guest connectivity is no longer something the lodges think about.

Staff communication

Over 800 Mbps measured across the reserve's own backbone, linking the main lodge, Mountain Retreat and Samar.

Security and operations

Daily provider callouts went to zero. Every fault used to need a vehicle and a person; now the network is monitored remotely.

Ownership

The reserve keeps adding systems on top of the backbone. In the client's words, they stopped doing speed tests.

Elephants broke out after 21:00 and staff had no effective way to coordinate. The requirement that came out of it: dependable communications after hours, across the areas where an incident can happen.

An Eastern Cape lodge near Addo
Why own it

What changes when the reserve owns its network

Today: a connection per lodge

  • Each lodge buys and manages its own service
  • Wi-Fi is listed for the public areas by the main lodge
  • Security, ecology and maintenance teams are not on a shared network
  • Nothing links the gates, water points or fences

With a reserve backbone

  • One uncontended carrier feed shared across the reserve
  • Lodges, HQ, the anti-poaching base and gates on one private network
  • Coverage out into the field, day and night
  • An owned asset that takes cameras and sensors without new towers

Avoided loss

Gate cameras, fence and trigger alarms, and after-hours communication for the Equine APU and K9 unit. When something happens at night, the right people know in minutes.

Operational efficiency

Water points, pumps and fuel tanks report their own status, so there are fewer vehicle trips just to check. Maintenance, ecology and lodges share one communications path.

Infrastructure ownership

High sites, backbone and power belong to the reserve. The network grows with Amakhala instead of depending on each lodge's separate provider.

Executive risk reduction

Management gets live visibility of the network, cameras and sensors, plus a record of operational diligence for owners, insurers and conservation partners.

Method. Terrain: Copernicus DEM GLO-30 (30 m). Imagery: ESA Sentinel-2 L2A true colour, 5 August 2026. Radio model: 5.8 GHz, effective earth radius factor 4/3, 60% first-Fresnel-zone clearance required at every point. Heights: carrier uplink 30 m, high-site masts 18 m, lodge masts 8 m, field terminals 3 m. The DEM does not model trees or buildings. Final paths are confirmed on survey and in Cambium LINKPlanner before anything is built.

Candidate positions. High Site South -33.56661, 26.07792; High Site North -33.52632, 26.08093; Safari relay -33.49751, 26.02860; carrier uplink -33.41625, 25.95175 (Paterson high ground). The exact carrier site is subject to Vodacom feasibility.
